extraction_notes.note: The proofs of Lemma bound_trace and of Master inequality I are written \begin{proof}[todo] with an empty body (the [todo] parses as an optional argument), and the proof of growth_ball is the single word 'todo', which cannot be located uniquely in the source; no proof nodes were emitted for them.

Placeholder environments whose whole body is '[todo]' are kept as nodes with that statement; their \labels could not be matched to the environments, so the uses edges from LP55 (cited by \ref in two proofs) were added by hand.

A proof environment follows Definition def:dart_of_pi (checking the dart-like axioms); the asserted fact was emitted as a claim nested in the definition, spanning the sentence 'we associate a dart-like structure ... by taking:', and the proof proves it.

Friedman's theorem, the expectation formula (Chen et al. Lemma 5.1), both master inequalities and the support bound are attributed to Friedman 2003 / Chen et al. 2025, so they are origin external although the blueprint (re)proves them; their proofs are paper.

Blueprint definitions of standard notions (finite graph, constant function, free group, ...) are kept origin paper as the project's formalisation targets; standard notions only recalled in running text (l^2, trace, Chebyshev polynomials, Fourier coefficients, distributions) are external 'standard (uncited)'.
Alon's conjecture is stated in one prose sentence ('most large regular trees' is presumably a slip for graphs); kept as an external conjecture resolved by Friedman's theorem.

The sentence 'Then Proposition \ref{thm:norm_adjacency_leq_sup_degree} is a trivial consequence of the following lemma' is the only proof of Theorem TP8 (the text calls it a Proposition); emitted as a prose proof using the following lemma.

Lean blueprint: many results have no proof or a placeholder proof ('Trivial.', 'todo', 'should be easily verified'); results whose proof gives no argument are marked rigor semi_formal, results with no proof environment at all are left formal.

Context sentences 'Let $G$ be a graph.' and generic parameter fixes ('We fix an integer $r \geq 1$.') were not made nodes; the ones that impose a hypothesis on a whole section (connected, locally finite, locally bounded) are assumption nodes.

nodes.statement: As in Graph, a \emph{graph} $G$ is a set of vertices $V(G)$, and a set of edges $E(G)$, such that each edge links two unordered, possibly identical vertices.
nodes.section: 1 Graphs: introduction and basic spectral theory
nodes.name: Graph (multigraph)
nodes.genus: a set of vertices $V(G)$, and a set of edges $E(G)$

nodes.statement: Note that this definition allows for loops (i.e. edges going from one vertex to itself) and multi-edges (i.e. multiple edges connecting two vertices).
nodes.section: 1 Graphs: introduction and basic spectral theory
nodes.name: Loops and multi-edges

nodes.statement: A \emph{dart} $d$ in a graph $G$ is an oriented edge, meaning it has a start point $\spt(d)$, and endpoint $\ept(d)$, is carried by an edge $\edge(d)$, and, in the case where $e$ is a loop, it has an additional information encoded in a boolean $\in \{0, 1\}$ encoding an orientation. We denote as $D(G)$ the set of darts on $G$.
nodes.name: Dart
nodes.statement_short: A dart is an oriented edge with start point, endpoint, carrying edge and (for loops) an orientation bit; $D(G)$ is the set of darts.
nodes.label: def:dart

nodes.statement: To each dart $d$ we associate a \emph{reverse dart} $\symm(d)$ such that: \begin{itemize} \item $\spt(\symm(d)) = \ept(d)$; \item $\ept(\symm(d)) = \spt(d)$; \item $\edge(\symm(d)) = \edge(d)$; \item if $\edge(d)$ is a loop then the orientation of $\symm(d)$ is the negation of the orientation of $d$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Reverse dart
nodes.statement_short: The reverse dart swaps start and end point, keeps the edge, and flips the loop orientation.
nodes.label: def:reverse_dart

nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item For any dart $d$, $\symm(d) \neq d$. \item For any dart $d$, $\symm(\symm(d)) = d$. \item We have a map $e \in E(G) \mapsto d_e \in D(G)$ such that, for all $e$, if $e$ links $x$ and $y$, then $d_e$ is a dart from $x$ to $y$ carried by $e$. \item For any $d, d'$, if $\edge(d)=\edge(d')$ then $d=d'$ or $d=\symm(d')$. \item We have $d_1 = d_2$ iff $\spt(d_1) = \spt(d_2)$ and $\edge(d_1) = \edge(d_2)$ (and same characterisation using the endpoints and edges). \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Dart API properties
nodes.statement_short: Basic dart properties: reversal has no fixed point, is an involution, edges lift to darts, darts on an edge are $d$ or its reverse.
conclusions: For any dart $d$, $\symm(d) \neq d$.
For any dart $d$, $\symm(\symm(d)) = d$.
nodes.label: lem:dart_API

nodes.statement: These depend on the implementation of darts, but should be easily verified.

nodes.name: Proof of Dart API properties

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$. The \emph{dartset} of $x$ is the set \begin{equation} \dartset(x) := \{ d \in D(G) \, : \, \spt(d)=x\}. \end{equation}
nodes.name: Dartset of a vertex
nodes.statement_short: The dartset of $x$ is the set of darts starting at $x$.
nodes.label: def:dartset

nodes.statement: \dartset(x) := \{ d \in D(G) \, : \, \spt(d)=x\}.
nodes.name: Dartset formula

nodes.statement: Let $x$, $y \in V(G)$. We define the dartset of $(x,y)$ as \begin{equation*} \dartset(x,y) = \{ d \in D(G) : \spt(d) = x, \ept(d) = y\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.name: Dartset of a pair
nodes.label: def:dartset_pair

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $x$ and $y$ are adjacent; \item there exists $d \in \dartset(x)$ such that $\ept(d)=y$; \item $\dartset(x,y)$ is not empty. \end{enumerate}

conclusions: The following are equivalent:

It is $2-1$ if $x=y$ and $1-1$ otherwise.

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set. A \emph{dart-like structure} on $V$ is the data of a set of darts $D$, together with maps $\spt, \ept : D \rightarrow V$ and $\symm : D \rightarrow D$ satisfying the following: \begin{itemize} \item $\spt \circ \symm = \ept$ and $\ept \circ \symm = \spt$; \item $\symm$ is an involution with no fixed point. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Dart-like structure
nodes.genus: the data of a set of darts $D$, together with maps $\spt, \ept : D \rightarrow V$ and $\symm : D \rightarrow D$
differentia: $\symm$ is an involution with no fixed point.
nodes.label: def:dartlike

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set and $D$, $\spt, \ept, \symm$ be a dart-like structure. We define a relation on $D$ by: \begin{equation*} \forall d, d' \in D, \quad d \sim d' \Leftrightarrow (d=d' \text{ or } d = \symm(d')). \end{equation*}
nodes.name: Dart equivalence relation
nodes.statement_short: Two darts are related when equal or reverse of each other.
nodes.label: def:dart_eq_rel

nodes.statement: The relation $\sim$ on $D$ is an equivalence relation, and all of its equivalence classes are of the form $\{d, \symm(d)\}$ (the two of which are distinct).
nodes.name: Dart relation is an equivalence
conclusions: The relation $\sim$ on $D$ is an equivalence relation, and all of its equivalence classes are of the form $\{d, \symm(d)\}$ (the two of which are distinct).
nodes.label: lem:dart_eq_rel

nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a set and $D$, $\spt, \ept, \symm$ be a dart-like structure. We define a graph $G$ associated to this structure by taking: \begin{itemize} \item $V(G) := V$ as the vertex set; \item $E(G) := D(G) \diagup \sim$ as the edge set; \item for $e \in E(G)$, if $d \in D(G)$ is a representant of $e$, then $e$ links $\spt(d)$ and $\ept(d)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Graph of a dart-like structure
nodes.statement_short: Vertices $V$, edges the classes of darts under $\sim$, an edge links the start and end of a representative.
nodes.label: def:graph_of_dart

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ constructed in Definition \ref{def:graph_of_dart} is a graph, and $D(G) = D$.
nodes.name: Darts of the graph of a dart-like structure

nodes.label: thm:dart_of_graph_of_dart

nodes.statement: A \emph{subgraph} $H$ of $G$ is a graph (of the same type as $G$) defined by: \begin{itemize} \item a vertex set $V(H)$ included in the vextex set of $G$ \item an edge set $E(H)$ included in the edge set of $H$ \item the same $\islink$ relation, i.e. if $e$ links $x$ and $y$ in $H$ then it also links $x$ and $y$ in $G$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Subgraph
nodes.label: def:subgraph

nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a subgraph of $G$. For any $x$, $y$ in $V(H)$, if $x$ and $y$ are adjacent for $H$, then they are adjacent for $G$.
nodes.name: Adjacency in a subgraph implies adjacency in the graph
conclusions: they are adjacent for $G$.

nodes.statement: We define the \emph{union} $H_1 \cup H_2$ of two subgraphs by taking the union of their respective vertex sets and edge sets, and the intersection $H_1 \cap H_2$ by taking their intersection.
nodes.name: Union and intersection of subgraphs
nodes.label: def:max_subgraph,def:min_subgraph

nodes.statement: A subgraph $H$ of $G$ is \emph{induced} if, for any $x, y \in V(H)$, for any $e \in E(G)$, if $e$ links $x$ and $y$ in $G$, then $e \in E(H)$.

nodes.label: def:isinduced

nodes.statement: Let $U$ be a subset of $V(G)$. Then we define a subgraph $H$ induced by $U$ by letting: \begin{itemize} \item $V(H) := U$; \item $E(H) := \{ e \in E(G) : \text{ both endpoints of }e \text{ lie in } U\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Subgraph induced by a vertex set
nodes.label: def:induced_subgraph

nodes.name: Induced iff induced from a vertex subset

nodes.statement: A graph $G$ is \emph{finite} if $V(G)$ and $E(G)$ are both finite sets.
nodes.name: Finite graph
nodes.label: def:finite

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$. We say $G$ is \emph{locally finite} at $x$ if $\dartset (x)$ is finite. The graph $G$ is \emph{locally finite} if it is locally finite at every vertex.
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.name: Locally finite graph
nodes.label: def:locally_finite

nodes.statement: Let $x$ be a vertex of $G$. The \emph{edegree} of $x$ is defined as $\mathrm{edeg}(x) = \# \dartset(x)$, which is an element of $\mathbb{N} \cup \{ \infty\}$. The \emph{degree} of $x$ is the natural-number projection of the edegree.
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.name: Degree and edegree
nodes.statement_short: The edegree of $x$ is the cardinal of its dartset in $\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$; the degree is its natural-number projection.
nodes.label: def:degree

nodes.statement: If $G$ is locally finite at $x \in V(G)$, then $\# \dartset(x,x)$ is an even number.
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.name: Loop dartset has even size
conclusions: $\# \dartset(x,x)$ is an even number.
nodes.label: lem:darset_loop_even

nodes.statement: Let $x \in V(G)$. $G$ is locally finite at $x$ iff $\incset(x)$ is finite, and in this case, \begin{equation*} \deg(x) = \# \incset(x) + \loopset(x). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.name: Degree via incident edges and loops
conclusions: $G$ is locally finite at $x$ iff $\incset(x)$ is finite
nodes.label: lem:degree_inc_loop

nodes.statement: Using Lemma \ref{lem:edge_range_of_darset}, \begin{align*} \deg(x) & = \sum_{y \in V(G)} \# \dartset(x,y) \\ & = 2 \# \{e \in E(G) : e \text{ links }x,x\} + \sum_{y \in V(G), y \neq x} \# \{e \in E(G) : e \text{ links }x,y\}\\ & = 2 \# \loopset(x) + (\# \incset(x) - \# \loopset(x)) \end{align*} which leads to the desired equality. Hence $G$ is locally finite at $x$ iff $\incset(x)$ and $\loopset(x)$ are both finite, which is equivalent to $\incset(x)$ being finite as $\loopset(x) \subseteq \incset(x)$.
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.statement_short: Count darts at $x$ via the 2-1 / 1-1 edge map, separating loops; finiteness follows since loops are incident edges.
nodes.name: Proof of Degree via incident edges and loops

nodes.statement: Let $\delta$ be a non-negative integer. We say $G$ is \emph{regular of degree $\delta$} if it is not empty, locally finite and, for every $x \in V(G)$, $\deg (x) = \delta$.
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.name: Regular graph
differentia: it is not empty, locally finite and, for every $x \in V(G)$, $\deg (x) = \delta$

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is regular of degree $0$ iff $E(G)=\emptyset$.
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.name: Regular of degree zero iff no edges

nodes.statement: We say $G$ is \emph{locally bounded} if it is locally finite and there exists a constant $D$ such that, for all $x \in V(G)$, $\deg(x) \leq D$.
nodes.section: 1.1.4 Locally finite graph, degree and regularity
nodes.name: Locally bounded graph
nodes.label: def:locally_bounded

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is \emph{bipartite} if there exists a partition $U_1$, $U_2$ of $V(G)$ such that, for all $e \in E(G)$, $e$ links an element of $U_1$ and an element of $U_2$.
nodes.name: Bipartite graph
nodes.label: def:bipartite

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. A \emph{dartwalk} from $x$ to $y$ on $G$ is given by a finite list $(d_1, \ldots, d_m)$ of darts, satisfying the following: \begin{itemize} \item $\spt(d_1)=x$ and $\ept(d_m)=y$; \item for any $i \in \{1, \ldots, m-1\}$, $\ept(d_{i+1}) = \spt(d_i)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.name: Dartwalk
nodes.label: def:dartwalk

nodes.statement: The \emph{length} of a walk is its number of darts.
nodes.name: Length of a walk
nodes.label: def:length

nodes.statement: The \emph{support} of the dartwalk $(d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ is the list $(x_i)_{0 \leq i \leq m}$ with $x_0=\spt(d_1)$ and $x_i = \ept(d_i)$ for $1 \leq i \leq m$.
nodes.name: Support of a dartwalk
nodes.label: def:dartwalk_support

nodes.statement: Let $w = (d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ be a dartwalk from $x$ to $y$ and $w' = (d_i')_{1 \leq i \leq m'}$ be a dartwalk from $y$ to $z$. We define the \emph{concatenation} $w \cdot w'$ to be the dartwalk $(d_i'')_{1 \leq i \leq m+m'}$ where $d_i''=d_i$ for $i \leq m$ and $d_{i-m}'$ for $i > m$.
nodes.name: Concatenation of dartwalks
nodes.label: def:concatenation

nodes.statement: The length of the concatenation of two dartwalks is the sum of their lengths.
nodes.name: Length of a concatenation
conclusions: The length of the concatenation of two dartwalks is the sum of their lengths.
nodes.label: lem:length_concat

nodes.statement: We define a binary relation on $V(G)$ by: $x \sim y$ if there exists a dartwalk from $x$ to $y$ on $G$. We then say $x$ and $y$ are \emph{reachable}.
nodes.name: Reachability
nodes.label: def:reachable

nodes.statement: The reachability relation is an equivalence relation on $V(G)$.
nodes.name: Reachability is an equivalence relation
conclusions: The reachability relation is an equivalence relation on $V(G)$.

nodes.statement: This is the same proof as in SimpleGraph.
nodes.name: Proof of Reachability is an equivalence relation

nodes.name: Adjacent vertices are reachable
conclusions: $x$ and $y$ are reachable.

nodes.statement: A dartwalk $(d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ is called a \emph{path} if for all $1 \leq i,j \leq m$, $\spt(d_i) = \spt(d_j) \Rightarrow i=j$.
nodes.name: Path
nodes.label: def:dartpath

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is a \emph{tree} if, for all $x$, $y \in V(G)$, there exists a unique path from $x$ to $y$.
nodes.name: Tree
nodes.label: def:tree

nodes.statement: A graph is \emph{preconnected} if any pair of vertices is reachable.
nodes.name: Preconnected graph
nodes.label: def:preconnected

nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is \emph{connected} if it is preconnected and $V(G)$ is not empty.
nodes.name: Connected graph
differentia: it is preconnected and $V(G)$ is not empty
nodes.label: def:connected

nodes.name: Connected iff some vertex reaches all
conclusions: The graph $G$ is connected if and only if there exists $x \in V(G)$ such that, for all $y \in V(G)$, $x$ and $y$ are reachable.

nodes.name: Connected component
nodes.label: def:connected_component

nodes.statement: For any vertex $x$, we define $\ccm(x)$ to be the unique connected component of $G$ containing $x$.
nodes.name: Connected component of a vertex
nodes.label: def:connected_component_Mk

nodes.statement: Let $x, y \in V(G)$. Then $\ccm(x) = \ccm(y)$ iff $x$ and $y$ are reachable.
nodes.name: Equal components iff reachable
conclusions: $\ccm(x) = \ccm(y)$ iff $x$ and $y$ are reachable.

nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a connected component of $G$. Then the subgraph induced by $C$ is connected.

conclusions: the subgraph induced by $C$ is connected.

nodes.name: Set of connected components

nodes.statement: A \emph{function} $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is a pair of functions $f_V : V(G_1) \rightarrow V(G_2)$ and $f_E : E(G_1) \rightarrow E(G_2)$. We will denote $f_V(x)=f(x)$ for $x \in V(G_1)$ and $f_E(e)=f(e)$ for $e \in E(G_1)$, i.e. view $f$ as a function from $V(G_1) \cup E(G_1)$ to $V(G_2) \cup E(G_2)$ sending vertices on vertices and edges on edges.
nodes.name: Function between graphs
nodes.label: def:function_graphs

nodes.statement: A \emph{morphism} $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is a function $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ such that for all $x, y \in V(G_1)$, $e \in E(G_1)$, if $e$ links $x$ and $y$ in $G_1$, then $f(e)$ links $f(x)$ and $f(y)$ in $G_2$.
nodes.name: Graph morphism
nodes.label: def:graph_morphism

nodes.statement: A morphism $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is an \emph{isomorphism} if there exist a morphism $g : G_2 \rightarrow G_1$ which is the inverse of $f$. In this case we denote $f^{-1}$ this inverse.
nodes.name: Graph isomorphism

nodes.name: Local isomorphism
nodes.label: def:local_isomorphism

nodes.statement: A morphism $f : G_1 \rightarrow G_2$ is a \emph{covering map} if it is surjective and a local isomorphism.
nodes.name: Covering map
nodes.label: def:covering_map

nodes.name: Covering graph

nodes.statement: Let $w = (d_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}$ be a dartwalk. We say $w$ \emph{admits a reduction} if there exists $1 \leq j < m$ such that $d_{j+1} = \symm(d_j)$. nodes.statement: We check that \begin{equation*} \spt(\symm(x,i,\epsilon)) = \spt(\pi_i^\epsilon(x),i,-\epsilon) = \pi_i^\epsilon(x) = \ept(x,i,\epsilon) \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \ept(\symm(x,i,\epsilon)) = \ept(\pi_i^\epsilon(x),i,-\epsilon) = \pi_i^{-\epsilon}(\pi_i^\epsilon(x)) = x = \spt(x,i,\epsilon) \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \symm(\symm(x,i,\epsilon)) = \symm((\pi_i^\epsilon(x),i,-\epsilon)) = (\pi_i^{-\epsilon}(\pi_i^\epsilon(x)),i,--\epsilon) = (x,i,\epsilon). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Check the two compatibility identities and the involution property directly.
nodes.name: Proof of Permutation darts form a dart-like structure

nodes.statement: Let $\Omega$ be an open subset of a real finite-dimensional normed space $E$ and $F$ be a real locally convex topological vector space.
nodes.name: Setting for distributions

nodes.statement: We denote as $\smooth[\Omega, F]$ the space of smooth functions $\Omega \rightarrow F$, and $\testfunc[\Omega, F]$ the set of smooth functions $\Omega \rightarrow F$ with compact support.
nodes.name: Smooth and test functions

nodes.statement: For $h \in \testfunc[\Omega, F]$, we denote as $\supp h$ its support.
nodes.name: Support of a function

nodes.statement: For $K$ a compact subset of $\Omega$ and $h \in \testfunc[\Omega, F]$, we write \begin{equation*} \|h\|_{C^m(K)} = \sup_{0 \leq k \leq m} \sup_{x \in K} |h^{(k)}(x)| \end{equation*} where $h^{(k)}$ is the $k$-th order derivative of $h$.
nodes.name: C^m norm on a compact

nodes.statement: We denote as $\distrib[\Omega, F]$ the space of classical distributions, i.e. continuous linear functionals $\nu : \testfunc[\Omega, F] \rightarrow F$. Here continuous means that, for any compact $K$ of $\Omega$, there exists a constant $C \geq 0$ and an integer $m \geq 0$ (both depending on $K$) such that \begin{equation*} \forall h \in \testfunc[\Omega,F], \quad \supp h \subseteq K \Rightarrow |\nu(h)| \leq C \|h\|_{C^m(K)}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Distributions: linear functionals on test functions bounded on each compact by a $C^m$ norm.
nodes.name: Distributions

nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a subset of $\Omega$. We say $\nu \in \distrib[\Omega, F]$ \emph{vanishes on} $A$ if, for all $h \in \testfunc[\Omega, F]$, if $\supp h \subseteq A$, then $\nu(h)=0$.
